outcomes.title: Direct Comparison Test
outcomes.description: Apply the direct comparison test to determine if a series converges or diverges.
outcomes.template:
Use the Direct Comparison Test to determine if \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \sum_{ n= {{k0}} }^\infty \frac{ {{top}} }{ {{bottom}} } converges.

Note that \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \frac{ {{top}} }{ {{bottom}} } is a positive, eventually decreasing sequence. We have that: \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} 0 \leq \displaystyle \sum_{ n= {{k0}} }^\infty \frac{ {{top}} }{ {{bottom}} } \leq \sum_{ n= {{k0}} }^\infty \frac{ {{simptop}} }{ {{simpbottom}} } =\sum_{ n= {{k0}} }^\infty \frac{ {{simpcoeff}} }{ n^{{P}} } which converges by the p-test since {{P}} > 1. So by the direct comparison text, \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \sum_{ n= {{k0}} }^\infty \frac{ {{top}} }{ {{bottom}} } converges.

Use the Direct Comparison Test to determine if \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \sum_{ n= {{k0}} }^\infty \frac{ {{top}} }{ {{bottom}} } converges.

Note that \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \frac{ {{top}} }{ {{bottom}} } is a positive, eventually decreasing sequence. We have that: \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \sum_{ n= {{k0}} }^\infty \frac{ {{top}} }{ {{bottom}} } \geq \sum_{ n= {{k0}} }^\infty \frac{ {{simptop}} }{ {{simpbottom}} } =\sum_{ n= {{k0}} }^\infty \frac{ {{simpcoeff}} }{ n^{{P}} } which diverges by the p-test since {{P}} \leq 1 So by the direct comparison text, \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \sum_{ n= {{k0}} }^\infty \frac{ {{top}} }{ {{bottom}} } diverges.

outcomes.title: Limit Comparison Test
outcomes.description: Apply the limit comparison test to determine if a series converges or diverges.
outcomes.template:

We can see that 0 < {{simpcoeff}} < \infty so by the Limit Comparison Test, \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \sum_{ n= {{k0}} }^\infty \frac{ {{top}} }{ {{bottom}} } converges if and only if \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \sum_{ n= {{k0}} }^\infty \frac{ 1 }{ n^{ {{P}} } } converges, which it does by the p-test since {{P}} > 1. outcomes.title: Alternating Series Test
outcomes.description: Determine if a series is absolutely convergent, conditionally convergent or divergent.
outcomes.template:

Determine if \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \sum_{ n= {{k0}} }^\infty (-1)^n \frac{ {{top}} }{ {{bottom}} } converges absolutely, converges conditionally or diverges.

Note that \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle |a_n| = \frac{ {{top}} }{ {{bottom}} }, b_n = \frac{1}{n^{ {{P}} } }. Note that a_n is a positive, eventually decreasing sequence. outcomes.template:
Find the interval of convergence for \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \sum_{ n= 0 }^\infty {{Cn}}({{linfact}})^n .

We begin with finding the radius of convergence R. By letting \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle b_n = {{Bn}}, we have that \renewcommand{\log}{\ln}\displaystyle b_{n+1} = {{Bnp1}}. We wish to find the values of x where \renewcommand{\log}{\ln}\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty} \left| \frac{b_{n+1}}{b_n} \right| \lim_{n\to\infty} \left| {{Bnp1}} \cdot {{Bnr}} \right| < 1 which occurs precisely when \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle |{{linfact}}| \lim_{n\to\infty} {{Ratio}} < 1, and by evaluating the limit, this occurs when \renewcommand{\log}{\ln}\displaystyle |{{linfact}}| {{Lim}} < 1, |{{linfact}}|< {{R}} or when \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle {{Lpoint}} < x < {{Rpoint}}.

To see if the series converges when \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle x={{Rpoint}}, we evaluate at \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle x={{Rpoint}}, to obtain the series \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty {{Rtest}} which {{rightprose}}s. (The student should perform the appropriate tests to confirm.)

To see if the series converges when \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle x={{Lpoint}}, we evaluate at \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle x={{Lpoint}}, to obtain the series \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty {{Ltest}} which {{leftprose}}s. (The student should perform the appropriate tests to confirm.)

So the interval of convergence is \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \left{{leftsymbol}} {{Lpoint}}, {{Rpoint}} \right{{rightsymbol}}.

Find the interval of convergence for \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle \sum_{ n= 0 }^\infty {{Cn}}({{linfact}})^n .

We begin with finding the radius of convergence R. By letting \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle b_n = {{Bn}}, we have that \renewcommand{\log}{\ln}\displaystyle b_{n+1} = {{Bnp1}}. We wish to find the values of x where \renewcommand{\log}{\ln}\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty} \left| \frac{b_{n+1}}{b_n} \right| \lim_{n\to\infty} \left| {{Bnp1}} \cdot {{Bnr}} \right| < 1 which occurs precisely when \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle |{{linfact}}| \lim_{n\to\infty} {{Ratio}} < 1, and by evaluating the limit, this occurs when \renewcommand{\log}{\ln}\displaystyle |{{linfact}}| \cdot 0 < 1 which occurs for all real numbers.

Thus the radius of convergence is R=\infty and the interval of convergence is \renewcommand{\log}{\ln} \displaystyle (-\infty, \infty) or \mathbb{R}.
